whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Identity and Access Management Architect exam?

personas.label: Identity architects
personas.description: You design how people and systems authenticate and want to demonstrate your Salesforce identity architecture skills.

personas.label: Integration specialists
personas.description: You build server-to-server connections and need to choose the OAuth flow that fits each integration.

personas.label: Security engineers
personas.description: You manage single sign-on, Connected Apps, multi-factor authentication, and session policy in Salesforce.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Identity and Access Management Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam asks you to choose among identity protocols and authentication flows that can look similar. Understand who starts a login, whether a user is present, and how an application protects credentials.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Protocol distinctions: Match SAML, OAuth, and OpenID Connect to their roles in a solution.
Single sign-on design: Know which system is the identity provider, how users are provisioned, and how Salesforce can provide identity to another app.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice sketching the OAuth flows and both SAML sign-on directions. Also review how Connected App scopes and policies work, and how the chosen MFA method fits with single sign-on.

examFormat.heading: Identity and Access Management Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test center. Questions describe sign-on, integration, or access requirements.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions present a login or integration scenario and ask which flow, policy, or identity feature fits. Look for whether a person is involved and whether the application can securely keep a client secret.
bestWayToPass: Compare OAuth flows: Review browser-based authorization, server-to-server JWT or client credentials, user-agent, and device authorization use cases.
Understand SAML roles: Practice service-provider-initiated and identity-provider-initiated sign-on, including Salesforce as an identity provider.
Review Connected App controls: Know scopes, user access policies, IP restrictions, session settings, and refresh token policies.
Plan MFA and provisioning: Understand supported verification approaches, just-in-time provisioning, and external account lifecycle management.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers Salesforce login and access architecture, including SAML single sign-on, OAuth flows, Connected Apps, multi-factor authentication, identity providers, and user provisioning. The exam is 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, with a 65% pass mark, weighted towards Accepting Third-Party Identity in Salesforce (21%) and Community (Partner and Customer) (18%).

keyConcepts.h2: Identity and Access Management Architect: core concepts

blocks.heading: Authentication, Authorization, and Identity
blocks.body: Authentication confirms who a user is. Authorization determines what an application or user may access. SAML is commonly used to exchange authentication assertions for single sign-on. OAuth provides delegated or application access through tokens without sharing a user password. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer to OAuth so an application can also learn who authenticated. Start a scenario by deciding whether it concerns identity verification, application authorization, or both.

blocks.heading: SAML Single Sign-On
blocks.body: The identity provider authenticates the user and issues an assertion; the service provider is the application the user wants to reach. In service-provider-initiated sign-on, the user begins at Salesforce and is redirected to the identity provider. In identity-provider-initiated sign-on, the user starts at the provider’s portal and opens Salesforce. Configure the trust values consistently, including the entity ID, certificate, and login URL. My Domain is part of Salesforce single sign-on setup. Certificate expiry, mismatched identifiers, and time differences can cause assertion failures. Salesforce can also act as an identity provider for other applications.

blocks.heading: OAuth 2.0 Flows
blocks.body: Choose a flow based on the client and the user interaction. The web server authorization-code flow suits a web application with a secure server that can protect its client secret. The user-agent flow is for clients that cannot keep a secret, such as a browser-based or mobile app. JWT bearer supports server-to-server access using a signed assertion, often without a user present. Client credentials can support server-to-server access tied to an integration user where available. Device authorization lets a user approve access on another device when the client has limited input. Refresh token policies determine how an application can renew access.

blocks.heading: Connected Apps, Scopes, and Policies
blocks.body: A Connected App registers an application that needs Salesforce access. OAuth scopes define the access the app requests, while policies determine which users can authorize or use it. Admin pre-authorization restricts use to configured users or permission sets; a self-authorized policy allows users to approve access under the org’s rules. Additional controls can include IP ranges, session settings, and refresh token policies. External Client Apps are another app-registration option in newer orgs. Revoking tokens prevents their further use.

blocks.heading: Provisioning, MFA, and My Domain
blocks.body: Identity design includes creating, updating, and removing user accounts as well as authenticating them. Just-in-time provisioning can create or update a Salesforce user from a SAML assertion at sign-in. SCIM and other user provisioning approaches can synchronize account lifecycle with an identity system. Multi-factor authentication can be satisfied by a supported Salesforce verification method or by an identity provider in a single sign-on setup when configured to meet Salesforce requirements. My Domain provides an org-specific login URL and supports identity features. Experience Cloud can support configured customer sign-on and self-registration options.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Identity and Access Management Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Identify whether a scenario concerns authenticating a person, authorizing an app, provisioning an account, or controlling a session. Then match the requirement to the protocol or feature.

blocks.heading: Select an OAuth Flow
blocks.body: Consider whether a person is present, whether the client can protect a secret, and whether the device has a browser. Use those details to compare web server, JWT bearer, client credentials, user-agent, and device flows.

blocks.heading: Check Both Sides of SAML
blocks.body: Confirm which system is the identity provider and which is the service provider. Check the entity ID, certificate, login URL, and My Domain setup for consistency.

blocks.heading: Apply Connected App Policies
blocks.body: Scopes limit requested token access. User policies determine who may connect, while IP and session settings add further controls.

blocks.heading: Plan MFA and Account Lifecycle
blocks.body: Know which authentication methods satisfy the org’s MFA requirements and how just-in-time provisioning or SCIM keeps user accounts aligned.

blocks.heading: Separate Login from Authorization
blocks.body: SAML and OpenID Connect help establish user identity; OAuth tokens grant application access. Some solutions use more than one protocol to cover both needs.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for identity architects
nextCertsAfter.intro: Build on identity and security work with a Salesforce architecture or integration credential.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main responsibility of an Identity and Access Management Architect?
options: Designing reports and dashboards for business teams
Create analytical reports for business teams
sampleQuestions.explanation: The role designs identity, sign-on, and access solutions for Salesforce and connected applications.
whyWrong: Email campaign design is a marketing task, not identity architecture.
Reporting does not address authentication or application access.
Workspace administration is not the role’s core identity focus.

sampleQuestions.question: Which standards are commonly used for Salesforce identity and sign-on?
options: SOAP web services for exchanging enterprise records
HTTP as the transport for browser requests
HTTP protocol for carrying web requests between systems
FTP for transferring identity files between servers
sampleQuestions.explanation: SAML and OAuth are widely used for single sign-on and application authorization.
whyWrong: SOAP is a service protocol, not the only identity standard.
HTTP carries requests but does not provide the sign-on protocol.
FTP transfers files and is not an identity standard.

sampleQuestions.question: What does My Domain provide in Salesforce?
options: A reports folder for organizing analytics
A custom dashboard theme without a login domain
A replacement for Salesforce access policies
sampleQuestions.explanation: My Domain provides an org-specific Salesforce URL and supports identity features.
whyWrong: Report folders organize analytics but do not provide a login domain.
Dashboard appearance is separate from the org-specific Salesforce URL.
This is the org-specific URL and identity foundation that My Domain provides.

sampleQuestions.question: Which capability lets a user authenticate once and access several configured applications?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Single sign-on lets users authenticate through a trusted identity setup and reach configured applications.
whyWrong: Roles affect record access and do not provide federated login.
Profiles assign permissions rather than authenticate across applications.
Permission sets grant permissions but do not provide single sign-on.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a primary purpose of a Connected App?
options: Connect only apps hosted inside Salesforce
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Connected App registers an application and configures scopes and policies for Salesforce access.
whyWrong: Email delivery is unrelated to OAuth app registration.
Connected Apps can support applications hosted outside Salesforce.
Connected Apps can use identity providers; they do not replace them.

sampleQuestions.question: In SAML single sign-on, what does the identity provider do?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The identity provider authenticates the user and sends an assertion the service provider can validate.
whyWrong: Permission assignment is authorization, not the IdP’s authentication function.
A profile is Salesforce authorization configuration.
Report hosting is not part of SAML identity exchange.

sampleQuestions.question: A headless application authenticates by signing a JWT assertion with its registered certificate and has no user session. Which OAuth flow applies?
options: Authorization-code flow for a browser login
User-agent flow for a public client
JWT bearer flow with a signed assertion
sampleQuestions.explanation: The JWT bearer flow exchanges a signed assertion for an access token, which supports server-to-server authentication without interactive user login.
whyWrong: Authorization-code flow includes a user authorization step.
User-agent flow is for clients that cannot protect a secret and involve user authorization.
Device flow is suited to a user authorizing a device on another screen.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a session security level control?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Session security levels distinguish the assurance expected for access to sensitive functions.
whyWrong: Timeout is a separate session setting.
Org-wide defaults control record sharing, not session assurance.
IP restrictions are separate from session security levels.

sampleQuestions.question: Which value can match an incoming SAML assertion to a Salesforce user?
options: Federation ID and mapped user attributes
Use a role name as the sole user identifier
Use a display name as the sole user identifier
Match users by display name as the only identity value
sampleQuestions.explanation: Federation ID commonly links an external identity to a Salesforce user; mapped attributes can also support provisioning.
whyWrong: Email may be used in some setups but is not the only possible identifier.
Role names do not uniquely identify users.
Display names may not be unique and are not a reliable identity key.

sampleQuestions.question: What does an Auth. Provider configuration do?
options: Creates users without an identity source
sampleQuestions.explanation: An Auth. Provider configures Salesforce to connect with an external identity service through supported protocols.
whyWrong: Provisioning may be configured separately; this is not the sole purpose.
Auth. Providers use protocols rather than replacing them.
Permission assignment is a separate authorization task.

sampleQuestions.question: What can satisfy Salesforce MFA requirements?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Salesforce MFA can use supported verification methods or a single sign-on provider configured to meet requirements.
whyWrong: SSO does not automatically satisfy MFA unless configured to do so.
OAuth grants application access but is not a second verification factor.
SAML sign-on alone does not necessarily provide the required second factor.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a Federation ID help establish?
options: Assigning permission sets to Salesforce users
sampleQuestions.explanation: Federation ID helps associate the Salesforce user record with the person’s identity at an external provider.
whyWrong: Permission sets grant access and are separate from identity matching.
OAuth scopes define application permissions, not user identity mapping.
Sharing rules govern record access rather than federated identity.

sampleQuestions.question: What should an architect consider when supporting multiple identity providers?
options: Routing or selection logic for the right provider
Force every user through a single provider
Let users manually configure each login
sampleQuestions.explanation: Domain-based routing or another selection method can direct users to the appropriate identity provider.
whyWrong: The requirement involves more than one provider.
Manual configuration is difficult to govern and scale.
Users need a defined provider to authenticate.

sampleQuestions.question: What is Certificate and Key Management used for?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certificates and keys support signed assertions and other secure trust relationships.
whyWrong: Account provisioning is a separate lifecycle process.
Profiles define permissions, not cryptographic trust.
Permission sets grant access and do not manage certificates.

sampleQuestions.question: Which practice supports identity governance?
options: Access reviews, least privilege, and audit logs
Grant broad access to simplify administration
sampleQuestions.explanation: Periodic reviews, limited access, and audit logs support accountable identity governance.
whyWrong: Without reviews, unnecessary access may remain.
Audit records support accountability and investigation.
Broad access conflicts with least privilege.

expertInsight: This exam rewards precision. Several OAuth flows can technically move a token around; but only one fits the situation described, and the deciding detail is usually whether a person is present and whether the app can keep a secret. Learn to spot those two things in the question. The other area worth drilling is SAML: know which side starts the login, and what breaks when the clock or the entity ID is wrong.
